To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hydrogen-bond network in the DNA binding pocket of the restriction endonucles EcoRI is essential for catalytic activity but does not affect the specificity for the recognition sequence -GAATTC-.
(a) The hydrogen-bonding interactions in the EcoRI-DNA complex are not essential for sequence recognition, but are required for efficient cleavage of the DNA backbone.
the hydrogen-bond interactions between the DNA recognition site and the two identical subunit of the dimer EcoRI are essential for catalytic activity of the enzyme.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanism by which EcoRI recognizes and cleaves its recognition sequence -GAATTC-.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of DNA cleavage by EcoR1.
the elucidation of the structural basis of the specificity and catalytic activity of EcoRI and other restriction endonucleases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hydrogen-bond network in the EcoRI DNA binding site is not essential for sequence specificity of this restriction enzyme but is essential for catalytic activity.

, in contrast to the expectation from the X-ray structure of EcoRI bound to DNA, the hydrogen bonding of the DNA binding sites of this enzyme to the recognition sequence -GAATTC-, in particular to guanine and the adjacent adenines, is not crucial for the sequence specificity of this restriction enzyme, but for its catalytic activity.
the DNA binding site mutants of EcoRI, investigated so far, do not lead to the recognition and cleavage of degenerate sequences, but to the loss of activity of the enzyme.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hydrogen-bonded interactions between the protein and the DNA are essential for the catalysis, but are not sufficient to ensure the specificity of the reaction.
the hydrogen bonds in the DNA binding sites of EcoRI are of utmost importance for catalysis, but not for specificity.
we have shown that the recognition of the sequence GAATTC by EcoRI is mediated by a total of 12 hydrogen bonds to the two identical subunit of the dimer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DNA binding site is a very sensitive region in EcoRI and any change in its hydrogen bonding potential leads to a significant reduction in the catalytic activity.
the DNA binding site mutations of EcoRI do not lead to any detectable loss in specificity.
we can use the EcoRI enzyme to study the effect of changing the hydrogen-bond potential of the DNA binding site on the specificity and catalytic activity of the enzyme.
